newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-ISU OFFICIAL SAYS OLYMPIC QUALIFYING RULE IS FLAW.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-ISU OFFICIAL SAYS OLYMPIC QUALIFYING RULE IS FLAW.

text.p: A top figure skating official has admitted there are flaws in a new qualifying points system for next year's Olympic and world events.
International Skating Union (ISU) vice-president Lawrence Demmy said on Thursday that the new system had not been thought through and was being abused and exploited.

It is also having the undesired effect of cutting the Olympic entries of major skating countries such as Russia, who can send only two men to Japan next year because Alexei Urmanov withdrew injured from Thursday's final.
Demmy said the rule would be changed but not before the middle of next year -- after the Winter Olympics and world championships had taken place.

He said the new system passed by the ruling body's biennial congress last year "was being abused and manipulated by some countries to facilitate increased representation next year, especially at the Olympics."
"Congress passed the rule last year by the required two-thirds majority but nobody thought it through to see it being manipulated for the following year," Demmy said.
"It is quite clear there is a problem with the present system and a change is required in Stockholm."
The Stockholm congress is scheduled for June 1998.
At least three countries did not bring their full entitlement of skaters to this week's world championships because to do so could reduce their entries next year at the Olympics.

Under the previous rule, a country which had a skater in the top three of an event at the world championships was entitled to three entries in that event -- and the Olympics when applicable -- the following year. If its best skater was between fourth and 10th, it was allowed two.
Under the new system, a country accumulates points based on its skaters placings in each event, with the total determining the number of entries the following year.
If the total adds up to more than 21 points, it can enter only two competitors the following year, regardless of where its best skater finished.
Any skater finishing worse than 15th or withdrawing after the official draw is made gets 16 points.
So with Alexei Yagudin and Ilya Kulik finishing third and fifth and Urmanov getting 16 points because of his withdrawal, Russia's men's total of 24 points limits the team to two entries next year.
The United States will also have only two men next year because Dan Hollander did not qualify for the main event.
Ukraine, Canada and Italy all decided not to bring a full team to Lausanne.
Ukraine withdrew former European champion Dmitry Dmitrenko as well as a dance couple and a pair before the draws were made because they were worried about the implications of the new rule.

"Yes we did so because of Olympic qualifying. We still have a strong team but we must think about the Olympic Games," Ludmila Mikhailovskaya, the president of the Ukraine Skating Federation, said on Thursday.
Her Canadian counterpart, David Dore, said Canada had withdrawn a dance couple for the same reason. Italy also held back a qualified dance couple this week.
Demmy said these countries were not breaking the rule, which was brought in to deal with the case of China's Chen Lu, the 1995 women's champion and 1996 runner-up.
He said that if Chen, China's only world-class skater, placed in the top three here, the old rule would have allowed her country to field three skaters at the Olympics.
"They might enter two skaters who can't skate," he said.
Demmy insisted that the new rule "was better than the old but it has opened the door for another problem.
"I wouldn't say it is a mistake. It is like anything not tried and tested," he said.
Earlier in the week, ISU president Ottavio Cinquanta criticised countries who left behind qualified skaters for the purposes of Olympic entry.
"My opinion is that is against the principle and ideal of sport and against the purpose the members had the previous year when they entered the skaters," he said.
